newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Saudi tycoon Khashoggi ventures into Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Saudi tycoon Khashoggi ventures into Chechnya.

text.p: Adnan Khashoggi, the globe-trotting Saudi business tycoon, announced plans on Friday to set up a joint investment bank to finance projects in Russia's breakaway Chechnya region and the Caucasus.

The Paris-based Saudi billionaire told Reuters during an international business forum in this Swiss mountain resort that the new Caucasus Investment Bank would have a paid-up capital of $100 million and be up and running by next year.

"This region is an opportunity for us. We are establishing business links with Chechnya and Georgia, with Russia's blessing of course," Khashoggi said during the annual Crans Montana forum which brings together political and business leaders.
The bank will focus on oil, transport and telecommunications projects in Chechnya and neighbouring Transcaucasus republics of Azerbaijan and Georgia as well as southern Russia, he said.
It will be based both in Chechnya and Georgia's capital Tbilisi, he added.
Asked his share in the bank's capital, Khashoggi said: "Very small. I'll put in $10 million."
Khashoggi and his Saudi partners would own 50 percent of the bank and the remainder by business groups in Chechnya and the Transcaucasus republics as well as investors from abroad.

Khashoggi said it was the first time he was venturing into business in the volatile Caucasus region on Russia's southern rim, where a bloody war in Chechnya between separatists and Russian troops killed tens of thousands of people.
Moscow withdrew its last troops early this year after failing to crush the separatists over 21 months of fighting but remains implacably opposed to their demands for independence.
Khashoggi said new business links would help to bring peace.
"Look what happened to Europe after World War Two. Trade helped Europe to stay together. Povery brings war," he said.
"You can't do business in that part of the world without security guarantees for investments," he added.

"The reason we are choosing Chechnya and Georgia is because they need a security programme so goods can come and go. We will go in to secure investments and shipments from ports. We'll open letters of credits," he said.

The Kremlin has vital interests in the oil-rich former Soviet Caucasus. Amidst a modern-day oil rush, some observers see a new Great Game in the making in the region where the British and Russian empires once competed for influence.

The Caspian Sea region stretching from Azerbaijan to western Kazakhstan and western Turkmenistan has vast oil and gas reserves and is witnessing intense pipeline politics involving the United States, Russia, Turkey and Iran.

Moscow is anxious to secure an oil pipeline that runs across the Chechen turf, and this month it signed a memorandum with Chechnya on transporting oil across its territory, advancing a bilateral peace deal and a huge international oil accord.
Russian oil pipeline monopoly Transneft owns the route that runs from the Caspian Sea to Russian Black Sea export outlets.

The deal could ease fears among the participants of the international oil consortium, Azerbaijan International Operating Company (AIOC), which has a deal with Transneft to carry its early oil to Novorossiisk in the Black Sea by October.
"Russia is a very important partner. Southern Russia will be part of this game," Khashoggi said.
Asked if he was afraid of Russian and Chechen mafia groups that roam the region, Khashoggi said: "We'll make them legitimate. We have to start somewhere, you know."
